speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what is the Ministry’s comparative assessment on the existing not-for-profit private acute hospital model in Singapore and those in other advanced economies in terms of (i) patient care (ii) talent development and (iii) alignment of institutional culture with the not-for-profit mission; (b) whether additional diversity in acute hospital models will complement Singapore’s existing care landscape; and (c) what factors might constrain the viability of entrants to this new industry locally and how can these be mitigated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not-for-profit hospitals are common around the world, such as in the United States (US), Netherlands, Japan, Korea.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It does not mean that they operate at a loss.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, all hospitals need to be financially viable, or they will have to close at some point.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A well-run not-for-profit hospital is sustainable in its operations, but do not distribute dividends to its shareholders.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, it ploughs back its profit to improve hospital services and facilities, and other activities such as charity.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are various reasons why hospitals would run as not-for-profit organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The key ones are that it is more in line with the public health mission of hospitals and it helps them access philanthropic funds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Apart from that, there are no major inherent differences in the way good for-profit and not-for-profit hospitals are run, in terms of quality of care, attention to value-based care, talent recruitment, development and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We see those qualities in Mount Alvernia Hospital, the only private, not-for-profit hospital in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) is consulting the industry to establish a next private hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, there will be stronger governance – it will be singularly licensed, that is, it will only have one healthcare licence, which means that the hospital operator needs to have strong oversight and control of its doctors’ clinical practices.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The various professionals – specialists, surgeons, general physicians, pharmacists, rehabilitation professionals – will have to work closer as a team to serve the patients.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We intend to specify these as conditions that potential hospital operators will have to meet and will be evaluated on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means that land price will not be the sole criterion in determining the hospital operator.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Why do we want to establish a new private hospital model with these key features?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The main reason is that it provides a better range of options in our healthcare landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, we have public healthcare which is heavily subsidised by the Government and which we try to make as affordable to Singaporeans as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the nature of subsidised care is there is a wait time, which can be quite lengthy for non-urgent electives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The public healthcare system is complemented by private healthcare services, where we have a range of hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most are quite high in cost and you need to be able to afford or be well-insured to access them, with little or no wait time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are a few private hospitals that are lower in cost, such as Mount Alvernia, some say maybe Raffles Hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH’s view is that we can increase options for lower-cost private hospitals so that private healthcare better complements public healthcare and we have a more adequate range of options for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: About 10 years ago, the share between public and private hospital workload was 85:15.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is good in the sense that it is a demonstration of the public’s confidence in public hospitals, but it is not so positive because it adds considerable load to the public healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are better off with a variegated system, where residents who are well-insured with private policies, have less need for subsidies, can opt for a lower-cost private hospital care if they wish to.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Private hospitals will also bring new insights and ideas to the management and delivery of healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The additional diversity will enrich and improve the quality of our healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOH has received good responses from various professionals and the industry after our invitation for consultation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I prefer not to make any pre-judgements on the constraints or success factors on this new private hospital model.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am sure we will receive many useful inputs and suggestions on how to help us improve and refine our model, and make it a success.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I should start by declaring that I work at a public hospital, although I have also worked in the past at a private hospital.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have two supplementary questions to the Minister.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Has the Ministry given consideration to what incentives will be needed, what approach will be needed to the culture of these hospitals and whether it will have any say in the leadership approach in these hospitals to ensure that the outcomes that the Ministry seeks will be achieved?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And may I suggest to the Ministry that although we do not want to prejudge the analysis, it is important to look at the drivers which shape whether certain models of care are viable, whether it is in terms of how the land cost is approached, how the tender is structured, including what backup measures there are to ensure that the institution does not drift from the intended purpose?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Mr Ong Ye Kung: The first question on leadership and culture, I fully agree.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Ultimately, that is the soul of the organisation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Without the right leadership, right culture, it will not serve our purpose.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As to what incentives there can be, I personally think it is difficult to have incentives or schemes that will ensure you have the right culture.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is fundamentally inherent in the soul of the organisation, but having said that, I think rules, regulations do matter.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As to why we did not think about the model earlier, I think there are practical considerations.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have been expanding our public healthcare and hospitals, and there is a need for manpower, for doctors.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As the Member knows, doctors and surgeons take time to develop and to mature and to be good in their skills.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The resource, in terms of manpower and talent, is limited.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we over push this, we can end up having a bidding war of our healthcare professionals and talent, which is why we are always careful as we develop our healthcare capacity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Having said that, between now and end of the decade, we are developing and building more public hospitals.
